content: Anaemia is a significant global public health issue, particularly affecting children under the age of five in developing regions, such as Africa and South-East Asia. While anaemia has multiple causes, malaria is a well-documented contributor to anaemia in children living in areas where malaria is endemic. Intermittent preventive antimalarial treatment (IPT) has been proposed as a potential intervention to reduce anaemia in these children. The rationale is that IPT could prevent new infections with Plasmodium parasites (the causative agents of malaria), thereby allowing haemoglobin levels to recover. The objective of this study was to evaluate the impact of IPT on children with anaemia residing in malaria-endemic regions. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and LILACS. Additionally, ongoing trials were identified through the World Health Organization (WHO) International Clinical Trial Registry Platform and the metaRegister of Controlled Trials (mRCT). The search was completed on December 4, 2014. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed the effects of IPT on children with anaemia. Data extraction and risk of bias assessment were performed independently by two reviewers. Meta-analyses were conducted, and data were stratified based on whether participants received iron supplementation. The quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Six trials, involving a total of 3847 participants, met the inclusion criteria. These trials were conducted in areas with varying levels of malaria endemicity: three in regions of low endemicity and three in regions of moderate to high endemicity. Four of the trials were conducted in areas with seasonal malaria transmission. In two trials, all children received iron supplementation, while two other trials used a factorial design to evaluate the effects of iron supplementation. The findings suggest that IPT for children with anaemia likely has little to no effect on the proportion of children who remain anaemic at 12 weeks of follow-up (based on four trials with 2237 participants; moderate-quality evidence). However, IPT probably increases the average change in haemoglobin levels from baseline to 12 weeks by 0.32 g/dL (mean difference [MD] 0.32, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.19 to 0.45; four trials, 1672 participants; moderate-quality evidence). Additionally, IPT may improve haemoglobin levels at 12 weeks (MD 0.35, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.64; four trials, 1672 participants; low-quality evidence). Subgroup analyses did not reveal significant differences between children who received iron supplementation and those who did not for these outcomes. Regarding mortality and hospital admissions, IPT likely has little to no effect at six months of follow-up (based on three trials with 3160 participants; moderate-quality evidence). Subgroup analyses again showed no differences between children receiving iron supplementation and those who did not. In conclusion, while the trials demonstrated a modest improvement in average haemoglobin levels with IPT, this did not appear to translate into reductions in mortality or hospital admissions. It is worth noting that three of the six trials were conducted in areas of low malaria endemicity, where the protective effects of IPT are expected to be limited due to lower transmission rates.
